---
title: "Puzzle #3 — Make Any Number of Right Triangles"
description: "A mathematical explanation of an Algorithmic Puzzles problem, from small cases to proof."
---

## 1. State the problem clearly

Can a rectangle be covered exactly by n right triangles, for every integer n greater than one, if triangles may have different sizes? The important word is EVERY, not just 'find a nice picture for four triangles'.

## 2. Start with the simplest useful observation

Cut a rectangle from one corner to the opposite corner. You immediately obtain TWO right triangles. What if we could always replace one right triangle by two smaller ones?

## 3. Express the relationship mathematically

$$
T(n)\Longrightarrow T(n+1)\qquad(n\ge2)
$$

**Explain every symbol:** T(n) means 'there exists a dissection of some rectangle into exactly n right triangles'. The arrow means if T(n) holds, then T(n+1) also holds. n is the current number of triangles.

**Substitute actual numbers:** Starting with n=2, split one existing right triangle into two right triangles by drawing the altitude from its right-angle vertex to its hypotenuse. The old piece is replaced by two pieces, so the count becomes 2−1+2=3. Do it again to get 4, and again to get 5.

## 4. Derive the answer and prove it works

The new line reaches the hypotenuse at a right angle, so BOTH smaller triangles are right triangles. It stays entirely inside the original piece, so it introduces neither gaps nor overlap. This establishes the induction step for every n≥2.

## 5. Check the result step by step

**Proof by induction:** Base case T(2) is true by a diagonal cut. Assume T(k) for some k≥2. Choose any right triangle in that dissection, split it as above, and obtain T(k+1). Therefore T(n) is true for every integer n≥2. There is no missing n in the allowed range.

## 6. What survives when the numbers change?

The same method illustrates constructive existence proofs: demonstrating that an object can be extended by one preserves a useful property. The choice of which triangle to split may change the shape, but not the argument.

## 7. Try it yourself

Why is it important to say the two new pieces remain right triangles? What would go wrong if we just drew an arbitrary line?

**Techniques:** Mathematical induction, construction, preservation of constraints..

**Book reference:** Levitin and Levitin, *Algorithmic Puzzles* (Oxford University Press, 2011), Easier #3, printed p. 32; hint p. 72; solution p. 83.. The explanation and formulation here are written independently.
